Science.summary: Replacing commonly used diversity, equity and inclusion-related terminology such as "belonging" with carefully matched alternative language may improve Republicans' favorability toward diversity training, according to new research from the ILR School.

Science.title: Drone-based AI system tracks cattle growth without stressful trips to scales
Science.summary: In beef cattle production, determining the ideal time to sell makes all the difference in a producer's costs. This is because, once an animal reaches its natural growth limit, it stops gaining weight significantly. From that point on, every additional day in a feedlot means spending money on feed without gaining meat in return.

Science.title: Supercharged 'molecule highway' membrane that speeds water transport could transform industrial processing
Science.summary: New membrane technology delivering faster and more precise molecule separation could improve the efficiency and sustainability of energy-intensive industrial processes—from purifying chemicals and recovering valuable resources to producing sustainable fuels.

Science.title: For many, striped bass fishing is a way of life. But the iconic species could face collapse
Science.summary: Striped bass fishing has been Bill Jakob's passion for more than 60 years, and he remembers an era when he'd spend all night casting his line into the crashing waves off Montauk and get eight or nine fish ranging up to 40 pounds (18 kilograms), a big catch by anyone's standards.

Science.title: Could AI ever build itself? Scientists map the road to the 'last AI built by humans.'
Science.summary: Researchers hope recursive self-improvement could tackle the skyrocketing costs of developing advanced AI models. But is it viable?

Science.summary: A biology student found a Native American stone spearpoint when searching for shark teeth along the coast of Virginia.

Science.summary: America’s newest aerospace expo and air show – MAX POWER – is fast approaching, and NASA has announced key events beginning Friday, Nov. 6, and running through Sunday, Nov. 8, hosted on and near the agency’s Kennedy Space Center in Florida. While scientists can never know for sure where a Martian meteorite originated, Teghaza 001 includes clues that link it to highlands in the southern hemisphere of […]

Science.title: Are dinosaur fossils hogging top journals? Analysis sparks debate over ‘charismatic’ finds
Science.summary: Nature, Published online: 30 October 2026; doi:10.1038/d41586-026-03512-2 Fossils of dinosaurs, mammals and other glamorous species are over-represented in high-profile titles, suggests a study of thousands of palaeontology papers.

Science.title: Hubble reveals a stunning twist in how the universe emerged from darkness
Science.summary: A surprising discovery by astronomers using the Hubble Space Telescope is challenging a leading explanation for how the early universe emerged from a dense fog of hydrogen roughly 13 billion years ago. Scientists once believed powerful winds from exploding stars helped radiation escape galaxies and clear that cosmic fog, but new observations reveal that these winds actually block radiation instead.

Science.title: November’s Night Sky Notes: Light-Day Away
Science.summary: Twin Travelers In 1977, NASA launched twin spacecraft Voyager 1 and 2, taking advantage of a once-every-175-year planetary alignment of the four largest planets in our solar system: Jupiter, Saturn, Uranus, and Neptune. Using six gravity assists between them, this Grand Tour gave us up-close views of the gas and ice giants, including several moons. […]

Science.title: A mysterious star system just 16 light-years away may be hiding habitable planets
Science.summary: Astronomers have solved a 170-year-old planetary mystery in a nearby two-star system, discovering that a mysterious wobble was caused by stellar activity rather than a giant planet. Although Jupiter-sized worlds have been ruled out in key regions, smaller, potentially habitable planets could still be waiting to be discovered just 16 light-years from Earth.

Science.title: Rediscovered 1935 recordings reveal earliest known spoken audio of endangered Louisiana Creole
Science.summary: The earliest spoken-word recordings of Louisiana Creole, a uniquely American language at risk of extinction, have been uncovered and analyzed for the first time, shedding light on a tongue that defined the docks and saloons of New Orleans for well over a century.

Science.title: Four new frog species reveal more of Peru's biodiversity
Science.summary: Science can't study a species—or unlock its potential to change the world—until people actually know it exists. Four new species of frogs have now been given names, thanks to the efforts of FIU biologist Alessandro Catenazzi.

Science.title: Scientists discover why chronic back pain feels so personal
Science.summary: A surprising discovery at UC San Diego suggests that chronic lower back pain may become deeply embedded in the brain's sense of personal identity. Researchers found that movement-triggered pain activates a brain network associated with self-awareness and memories, even though ordinary acute pain typically shuts this network down. This unexpected difference could explain why conventional pain medications often provide limited relief and why fear, anticipation, and past experiences can intensify chronic pain.

Science.title: Scientists discover mysterious seahorse lookalikes that no one has ever seen alive
Science.summary: Scientists have discovered that three bizarre deep-sea fish that look exactly like seahorses actually belong to a separate evolutionary group, proving that nature created the same unusual body shape more than once. Nicknamed "sea muppets," these elusive creatures are known from just seven specimens, and no one has ever seen one alive.

Science.title: A gamma-ray powerhouse's smoking gun? Gas trail points to microquasar jets
Science.summary: In 2016, a binary star system emitting unusually strong gamma rays was discovered in our galactic neighborhood. Now, astronomers have found the smoking gun, or rather, a smoking trail of cool molecular gas that suggests jets emanating from a microquasar—one of the few known outside the Milky Way—are responsible.

Science.title: A decade of carbon dioxide data from space gets an upgrade
Science.summary: Every day, two NASA space instruments known as the Orbiting Carbon Observatory-2 and -3 (OCO-2 and OCO-3) capture more than a million observations of sunlight reflecting off Earth's surface. Using the physics of how light travels through the air, an algorithm converts these raw data into atmospheric carbon dioxide (CO₂) concentrations.

Science.title: Global wildlife trade is twice previous species estimates, but major data gaps suggest true scale is even larger
Science.summary: More than 107,000 species are used and traded worldwide, more than double previous estimates, according to new research that suggests the true scale may be far greater due to major gaps in trade and wildlife collection data.

Science.title: What the Cornell 7 sexual assault allegations reveal about how parents talk to their kids about rape
Science.summary: There is approximately 60 years of research on campus sexual assault and shelves full of books on young people's sexual experiences and behaviors, including their experiences with assault.

Science.title: New home for orangutans rescued from Indonesia's burning forests
Science.summary: Deep in a forest in Indonesian Borneo, conservationists open a cage. A female orangutan and her baby waste little time, clambering up the towering trees and disappearing into the canopy, safe at last.

Science.title: The bonus that makes employees more committed
Science.summary: Offer your employees money to quit and the ones who say no will work harder as a result. Researchers at the University of Waterloo, Wilfrid Laurier University and McMaster University set out to test whether pay-to-quit programs work as intended. Their results confirmed they do and revealed a benefit that nobody anticipated.

Science.title: Tiny photonic chip links telescopes together to view the universe in 'astonishing' detail
Science.summary: A tiny glass chip developed by researchers at Heriot-Watt University has linked two telescopes together to enable them to act as a single powerful instrument, marking an important step toward a new generation of astronomical technology.

Science.title: Record-breaking retraction: scholarly publisher pulls 1,400 conference papers on one day
Science.summary: Nature, Published online: 30 October 2026; doi:10.1038/d41586-026-03455-8 Announcement by IEEE follows publication of a study showing the retracted papers are linked to paper mills.

Science.title: An aquanaut comes home: Returning to Earth from an undersea 'space station'
Science.summary: After five days of living underwater, Analog Astronaut Commander Dr. Musilova and her crew return to terra firma, affected by higher pressures and the team's disconnection from home.

Science.title: UTe₂ reveals two flavors of superconductivity under extreme pressure
Science.summary: Quantum researchers are searching for a topological superconductor—a material that, if discovered, would allow major advances in quantum computing by combining two distinct "flavors" of superconductivity.

Science.title: Figuring out where cosmic neutrinos come from is tricky—radio telescopes could help find 'ghost particles' origin
Science.summary: Neutrinos are funny little particles that weigh almost nothing, making them one of the universe's most elusive building blocks. They can come from objects as mundane as bananas and as exotic as supernovas—the exploding death throes of massive stars. Most neutrinos stream through space and pass through the Earth without interacting with anything.

Science.title: Neuroscientists reveal method to train people to have lucid dreams — and it involves virtual reality and meditation
Science.summary: People who had no recollection of a lucid dream over the past three years developed the skill after one month of performing a novel training regimen twice a week, neuroscientists report.

Science.title: Somewhere over the transcontinental burrito tunnel
Science.summary: Nature, Published online: 30 October 2026; doi:10.1038/d41586-026-03368-6 Pipe dreams.

Science.title: 'Star Trek's' William Shatner and George Takei honor the death of Walter Koenig
Science.summary: 'Rest well, my dear friend. Keep navigating a steady course.'

Science.title: Livestock guardian dogs enlisted in efforts to conserve Texas' smallest fox
Science.summary: In the Texas Panhandle, two livestock guardian dogs patrol a herd of cattle grazing the Rita Blanca National Grasslands. Although their singular focus is protecting the herd from would-be predators, their presence may make them wildlife conservation allies.

Science.title: What killed 500-plus penguins? How scientists solved the mystery
Science.summary: The penguins that perished lived on the Danger Islands in Antarctica. The prime suspect was avian flu. Researchers were surprised by what they found.

Science.title: Are narcissists multiplying or is the social media algorithm making them bolder? The answer in five stages
Science.summary: Social media doesn't necessarily reflect who you are, but it may intensify particular personality traits and confirm or even persuade you that your worst behavior is justified.

Science.title: Artemis II commander Reid Wiseman named deputy director for NASA's Jet Propulsion Laboratory
Science.summary: The leader of NASA's first mission around the moon in half a century is the last to announce what's next for him after retiring from active astronaut duty.

Science.title: Q&A: Deep learning–enhanced air quality monitoring achieved using satellite data
Science.summary: A doctoral dissertation by Andrea Porcheddu, MSc in the field of Technical Physics will be examined at the Faculty of Science, Forestry and Technology, Kuopio campus.

Science.title: The rocket scientist who summoned demons: The true horror story of Jack Parsons
Science.summary: Rocketry pioneer Jack Parsons engaged in an elaborate series of occult ceremonies intended to summon an otherworldly feminine goddess into physical existence.

Science.title: Novel chemical reaction expands options for building DNA-encoded libraries
Science.summary: Finding new drugs requires screening vast numbers of compounds to identify those that interact with a biological target. DNA-encoded libraries (DELs) help researchers explore these large collections by attaching a short DNA sequence to each molecule, acting as a molecular barcode that allows compounds with promising properties to be identified.

Science.title: Chemists create disappearing tattoos: Here's the science behind how they work
Science.summary: How handy would it be if you could make your tattoos invisible for a job interview in the morning, and reveal them again for a party in the evening? This sounds like science fiction, but it may soon be reality.

Science.title: Hauntology examines how what happened in the past—and what didn't—informs the present
Science.summary: The spooky is a hugely popular phenomenon in British culture, demonstrated in what now seems like a month-long Halloween celebration, a rich tradition of horror cinema and a growing interest in the uncanny. But there are other manifestations of haunting.

Science.title: Read an extract from Dark Eden by Chris Beckett
Science.summary: In this extract from Chris Beckett’s Dark Eden, the November read for the New Scientist Book Club, we meet some of the inhabitants of a dark planet that drifts outside the Milky Way, descendants of two astronauts marooned there over a century earlier

Science.title: Vega Island Frozen in Fright
Science.summary: The sight of an icy skull-like visage on the Antarctic island could make one’s blood run cold.

Science.title: Think Halloween is scary? This scorched alien world is a real-life cosmic horror story
Science.summary: Earth would be terrifying if we celebrated Halloween every 11 hours, a possibility on a super-Earth investigated by the JWST, if it wasn't so hellishly hot that no life could survive on its surface.

Science.title: How a 'tropical' shortcut could help particle collider experiments
Science.summary: Particle accelerators are expensive. Not just to build or to run, but also to predict the outcome of measurements obtained from them.

Science.title: Bright object beyond Pluto may be the solar system's sixth dwarf planet
Science.summary: The Vera C. Rubin Observatory has found what might be a new dwarf planet in our solar system, orbiting the sun on an inclined plane past Pluto.

Science.title: Physicists created a tiny universe and watched time emerge without a clock
Science.summary: Scientists have created a miniature universe in the laboratory that could help answer one of the biggest mysteries in physics: What is time, and where does it come from? Using 24,000 ultracold atoms, a University of Birmingham researcher built an isolated quantum system that repeatedly expands and contracts, mimicking the Big Bang and a possible Big Crunch. Remarkably, the experiment showed that time could emerge from changes happening inside the system, without relying on an external clock.

Science.title: Ancient copper mine hints that Iberia played an important role in Bronze Age trade networks
Science.summary: Copper is essential for making bronze, which shaped tools, weapons and ornaments across Bronze Age Europe. While many Bronze Age mines have been identified throughout Europe, researchers are still trying to pin down which of them were most active at different times and how far their copper traveled. New research, published in the journal Antiquity, suggests that a series of mines in modern-day Spain and Portugal may have been an important source of copper in the Late Bronze Age, with some of that copper ending up as far away as Scandinavia.

Science.title: 'Crystal Lake' is great, but nothing tops the space horror shenanigans of 'Jason X'
Science.summary: The Voorhees legend continues in Crystal Lake, but Jason X remains the Citizen Kane of this franchise.

Science.title: The asteroid killed the dinosaurs. Why did crocodiles survive?
Science.summary: Scientists may have solved a 66-million-year-old mystery: how crocodiles survived the asteroid that wiped out the dinosaurs. A sweeping analysis of fossils and ancient climates suggests that their preference for warm environments placed them in tropical refuges that remained habitable even after the catastrophic impact.

Science.title: Briefing Chat: Dog years: could longevity science extend your pets' lives?
Science.summary: Nature, Published online: 30 October 2026; doi:10.1038/d41586-026-03553-7 Nature staff discuss the emerging field of pet longevity — plus, a researcher decides not to care about their student reviews. Are they wrong?

Science.title: The Taurid meteor shower isn't much to look at. That's why I love it
Science.summary: The Taurids produce only a handful of meteors an hour. That sounds disappointing, but I've learned that expecting almost nothing can make this one of the most enjoyable meteor showers of the year.
